title: Module 2 Misconception Sort
intro: Decide whether each statement is true, false, or depends. These are the misconceptions that cost students points on exams.

items.s: The mean is always the best measure of central tendency.
items.why: With strong skew or outliers the median is usually a better summary of a typical case.

items.s: In a positively skewed distribution the mean is usually larger than the median.
items.why: The long tail of high scores pulls the mean toward it. The median resists extreme scores.

items.s: The standard deviation is the average of the deviation scores.
items.why: The average of deviation scores is zero. The standard deviation squares the deviations first, averages them, and takes the square root.

items.s: A distribution can have more than one mode.
items.why: Two or more scores can tie for the highest frequency. We call such distributions bimodal or multimodal.

items.s: A larger standard deviation means the scores are more spread out.
items.why: That is its purpose. Compare standard deviations only for the same variable measured the same way.

items.s: You can compute a meaningful mean for any variable that has numbers attached.
items.why: Numbers that label categories, such as jersey numbers or diagnosis codes, have no meaningful mean.

items.s: Adding one extreme score to a data set changes the median as much as it changes the mean.
items.why: The median shifts by at most one position in the ordering. The mean moves with the size of the extreme value.

items.s: Whether you report the mean or the median for household income
items.why: Income is usually positively skewed, so the median describes a typical household better. It depends on what you want to communicate and on the shape of the data.
